theorem Etingof.Proposition_2_2_3 (M : Type*) [MulOneClass M] (e : M) (he_left : ∀ a, e * a = a) (he_right : ∀ a, a * e = a) : e = 1. The book says 'if a unit exists, it is unique'. The theorem takes an arbitrary element e satisfying both left- and right-unit laws and deduces e = 1 (the canonical unit). This is the correct uniqueness statement. Proof is short (simp at this; exact this) but the statement is right.

Two theorems. (i) If V₁ is IsSimpleModule R and φ : V₁ →ₗ[R] V₂ with φ ≠ 0, then Function.Injective φ. (ii) If V₂ is IsSimpleModule R and φ : V₁ →ₗ[R] V₂ with φ ≠ 0, then Function.Surjective φ. The book states Schur's lemma exactly this way — nonzero hom from an irreducible is injective, to an irreducible is surjective, hence iso if both irreducible. The corollary (isomorphism when both irreducible) is a direct consequence of (i)+(ii) and is not a missing conjunct. The book works over 'any field F (not necessarily algebraically closed)'; the Lean statements use [Ring R] without field or algebraic closure, which is actually more general. Verified.

Part (i) — theorem Etingof.Proposition_2_7_1 [CharZero k] [NoZeroDivisors k]: LinearIndependent k (fun p : ℕ×ℕ => WeylAlgebra.monomial k p.1 p.2) ∧ ⊤ ≤ Submodule.span k (Set.range (fun p => WeylAlgebra.monomial k p.1 p.2)). This is exactly 'the monomials xⁱyʲ form a basis'. The CharZero and NoZeroDivisors hypotheses are mathematically necessary: over a characteristic-p field the Weyl algebra is not the same object and the basis claim is false. The book's proof also uses characteristic-0 reasoning (the module E = tᵃk[a][t,t⁻¹]). Part (ii) — theorem Etingof.Proposition_2_7_1_ii: LinearIndependent k (qMono k q) ∧ (qWeylAlgebra k q).toSubmodule = Submodule.span k (Set.range (qMono k q)). This covers all q ∈ kˣ with no char constraint, matching the book. Both parts faithful.
